title: Last weekend
title_target: Το περασμένο Σαββατοκύριακο — Toh peh-rah-smeh-noh Sah-vah-toh-kee-ryah-koh
goal: Complete the past tense with the regular patterns — six short rules that cover hundreds of verbs at once.
bekal: form the regular past from six ending patterns
know when the έ- prefix appears and when it drops
tell about a weekend from start to finish
praise and react to other people's stories

dialogs.title: ΔΙΑΛΟΓΟΣ — A day on Aegina
dialogs.intro: Ana is back from the island and tells Eleni about it. Every past verb in this dialog is **regular** — after this unit you can form almost all of them yourself without memorizing them one by one.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Amazing! We went to Aegina with Nikos.
lines.literal: amazingly! we-went — to-the — Aegina — with — the — Nikos.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: We swam all day, then bought pistachios.
lines.literal: we-swam — all — the — day, and — after — we-bought — pistachios.

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: Aegina is famous for its pistachios!
lines.literal: the — Aegina — it-is — famous (f) — for — the — pistachios — its.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Now I know! I also chatted with an old lady at the market.
lines.literal: it — I-know — now! I-spoke — also — with — a — granny — at-the — market.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Yes! I was so happy. I worked three months for that moment.
lines.literal: yes! I-was-glad — too — much. I-worked — three — months — for — it.

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: Well done! Did you take photos?

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Of course. And I read a little on the boat.
lines.literal: of-course. and — I-read — a-little — on-the — boat.

notes: **The regular past is formed by swapping the present ending according to the last letter of the stem.** Every pattern comes down to a **-σα** sound in various disguises: -σα, -ψα, -ξα, -ησα. The rest of the endings are exactly as in the last unit: -α, -ες, -ε, -αμε, -ατε, -αν.

**The έ- prefix appears ONLY when the word needs a place for its stress.** γράφω → **έ**γραψα (just two syllables, needs the prefix) but αγοράζω → αγόρασα (already four syllables, doesn't). ⚠️ And the prefix **drops again** as soon as the ending gets longer: **έ**γραψα but γρ**ά**ψαμε, **έ**κοψα but κ**ό**ψαμε. The rule is always one and the same: past-tense stress sits on the third syllable from the end.

**-μαι verbs have their own past ending: -ηκα.** κουράζομαι → κουρ**άστηκα**, σηκώνομαι → σηκ**ώθηκα**, κοιμάμαι → κοιμ**ήθηκα**, χαίρομαι → χ**άρηκα**, ετοιμάζομαι → ετοιμ**άστηκα**. ⚠️ These look strange at first, but the endings are perfectly regular: -ηκα, -ηκες, -ηκε, -ήκαμε, -ήκατε, -ηκαν.

**Χάρηκα has a second life as a set phrase.** *Χάρηκα!* means "nice meeting you" when parting, and **Χάρηκα πολύ** is the past version of the *Χαίρω πολύ* you used in unit 1. It's what you say as an introduction wraps up.

**Μπράβο σου!** — "good for you!". Note the **σου**: Greek praise is aimed at the person, not the deed. The polite form is *Μπράβο σας!* ⚠️ The word is borrowed from Italian and used far more often than in English — for a child who finishes their food, or a foreigner who manages one Greek sentence.

**Τραβάω φωτογραφίες** literally "pull photos", the Greek version of *take a picture*. Its past is **τράβηξα** — note the -άω pattern turning into -ηξα, not -ησα. It's a small group: τραβάω → τράβηξα, πετάω → πέταξα, φυλάω → φύλαξα.
**Δηλαδή** (*dhee-lah-DHEE*) = "that is, meaning". A very common linking word for summing up or asking for clarification. On its own, *Δηλαδή;* means "meaning what?".

**Τα φιστίκια Αιγίνης** are the pride of Aegina, an island just an hour from the port of Piraeus. ⚠️ English *pistachio* and Greek *φιστίκι* both go back to Persian — the same route that gave us παράδεισος and *paradise*.

grammars.title: Six regular past patterns
body: Look at the last letter of the verb's present stem, then follow its row. This covers most of the verbs you'll meet.
after: ⚠️ **A small set of -άω verbs uses -ξα, not -ησα**: τραβάω → τράβηξα, πετάω → πέταξα, φυλάω → φύλαξα. Just recognize them when you meet them; you can count them on one hand.

**These past stems are the same as the stems after να.** αγοράσω / αγόρασα, δουλέψω / δούλεψα, μιλήσω / μίλησα. So each past form you learn also gives you the να form and the future form — three for the price of one.

grammars.title: The past of -μαι verbs
body: The group with the oddest present endings turns out to be the most uniform in the past.
after: Others follow the same pattern: σηκώθηκα, πλύθηκα, ντύθηκα, ετοιμάστηκα, χάρηκα, λυπήθηκα, φοβήθηκα, θυμήθηκα, κοιμήθηκα.
⚠️ **Έρχομαι stays irregular**: ήρθα, not *ερχόμουν* — that one is a different past form you don't need yet.

blocks.text: Telling is only half a conversation. These ten reactions make you sound like someone really listening, not just waiting for a turn to talk.

blocks.title: The regular verbs you'll use most for telling stories
items: **αγοράζω → αγόρασα** buy · **διαβάζω → διάβασα** read · **δουλεύω → δούλεψα** work · **ταξιδεύω → ταξίδεψα** travel · **μαγειρεύω → μαγείρεψα** cook
**μιλάω → μίλησα** speak · **ρωτάω → ρώτησα** ask · **απαντάω → απάντησα** answer · **κολυμπάω → κολύμπησα** swim · **βοηθάω → βοήθησα** help
**γράφω → έγραψα** write · **ανοίγω → άνοιξα** open · **ψάχνω → έψαξα** look for · **αλλάζω → άλλαξα** change · **αρχίζω → άρχισα** begin · **τελειώνω → τελείωσα** finish
⚠️ **Καταλαβαίνω → κατάλαβα** (understand) looks regular but actually shrinks. *Κατάλαβα!* — "got it!" — is one word you'll say hundreds of times.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right past form for the subject.
Put the words in the right order.

items: I bought pistachios at the market.
I chatted with an old lady.

answers: αγόρασα — δούλεψα — έγραψα — μίλησα — άνοιξα — κουράστηκα
Πώς πέρασες το Σαββατοκύριακο; — Κολυμπήσαμε όλη μέρα. — Μίλησα με μια γιαγιά. — Χάρηκα πάρα πολύ. — Τράβηξες φωτογραφίες;
Κολυμπήσαμε όλη μέρα. — Αγόρασα φιστίκια στην αγορά. — Μίλησα με μια γιαγιά. — Κουράστηκα πολύ χθες. — Μπράβο σου!
